# 1 · Cloud-free composite {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## The problem, and it is ours specifically

Half the year, Indonesia is under cloud.

. . .

One image is a lottery. So we do not use one image — we take **every** image
over a period and keep, per pixel, the ones that were clear.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## A composite is not a photograph
No single moment exists in it. Every pixel may come from a different day, and
that is the point.
:::

## What to watch for

```js
.filterDate('2024-01-01', '2024-12-31')
.filterBounds(aoi)
.map(maskS2clouds)
.median()
```

. . .

- **too short a period** → holes where it was never clear
- **too long** → you average across real change
- `.median()` rather than `.mean()` — one bright cloud edge does not drag the
  answer

## Why `max: 3000`, not 255

Sentinel-2 reflectance is stored scaled — values run to several thousand, not
0–255.

. . .

Set `max: 255` and almost everything saturates white. Set it to 3000 and the
land looks right.

. . .

**This is a display choice, not a correction.** The numbers underneath never
changed — you are choosing how to stretch them onto a screen.

# 2 · NDVI {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## One subtraction, and why it works

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.5em; margin:.6em 0 .4em;"}
NDVI &nbsp;=&nbsp; ( NIR − Red ) &nbsp;÷&nbsp; ( NIR + Red )
:::

<!-- Written as text, not LaTeX, on purpose: Quarto pulls MathJax from a CDN,
     and one formula is not worth a live network dependency mid-webinar. If the
     connection drops, this still reads. -->

. . .

Yesterday: vegetation reflects ~5% of red and ~50% of near infrared. NDVI is
just that gap, **normalised so brightness cancels**.

. . .

A shaded hillside and a sunlit one give the same NDVI for the same plant.
That is why we divide.

## Reading the number

| NDVI | usually |
|---|---:|
| < 0 | water |
| 0 – 0.2 | bare soil, built-up |
| 0.2 – 0.5 | grass, crops, shrub |
| > 0.5 | dense vegetation |

::: {.fragment}
Ranges overlap and shift by season and sensor. Treat them as a starting point
to check, never as a classification.
:::

# 3 · Classification {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## The step nobody can copy from me

Everything else today you can paste. **Training points you must draw
yourself**, because they describe *your* district.

. . .

- 20–40 points per class is enough to start
- spread them out — not all from one corner
- pick pixels you are **certain** about; a doubtful point teaches the
  classifier something false

## Then 70 / 30

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Train on 70% of your points. **Hold back 30%** and let the classifier answer
those blind.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment}
If you test on the points you trained with, you measure memory, not skill —
and it will look excellent.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Read the accuracy before you look at the map
In that order. The map is persuasive whether or not it is right.
:::

## Because this always looks convincing

![](img/classification.svg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

::: {.fragment}
Crisp boundaries. Sensible colours. **None of that is evidence.**
:::

## Where your error will be

Look again at the middle panel: vegetation and water sit far apart, **bare
soil and settlement overlap**.

. . .

Both are dry, bright, moderate in the infrared. Their numbers genuinely
resemble each other.

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## When accuracy stalls around 80%
It is almost never the algorithm. Find the two classes sitting on top of each
other, then either add a band that separates them — shortwave infrared often
does — or merge them and say so in your report.
:::

# 4 · Change detection {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## Two dates, one subtraction

Build the same composite for two years. Subtract the NDVIs.

. . .

Negative means vegetation lost between the two dates.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## −0.15 is a choice, not a truth
Move the threshold and the area of "change" moves with it. Report the number
you used, and show what happens at one step either side.
:::

## Change that is not change

Before believing any loss patch, rule out:

- **different season** — a harvested paddy is not deforestation
- **cloud shadow** in one of the two composites
- **one bad year** — drought looks like clearing at this resolution

. . .

The honest check is a third date. If the loss persists, it is real; if it
returns, it was a season.

# 5 · Export {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## `Export` does not export

Running the line creates a **task**. Nothing leaves Earth Engine until you
open the Tasks tab and press **Run**.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The most common lost half-hour of the day
People run the script, see no error, and wait for a file that was never
requested.
:::

## And this is where the quota bites

You are asking for real pixels now, not a picture of them.

. . .

- set `scale` deliberately — 10 m over a whole province is enormous
- set `region` to your district, not the map view
- `maxPixels` exists to stop an accident, not to be raised reflexively

. . .

Exports land in **your Google Drive**, and can take minutes to hours.

# Your turn · 10 minutes {background-color="#0f3d2e"}

## Make it your own

1. change the area to **your** district
2. change the two years to ones you care about
3. run classification and change detection
4. start one export

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## When it breaks — and it will
Read the error's **first line** only. Nine times in ten it is a client/server
mistake, and yesterday's rule solves it.
:::

## After today {background-color="#f7f9fb"}

- the scripts stay online — copy, adapt, break them
- the reference page lists every dataset we touched
- accuracy below 70%? more training points first, more classes second

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## The one habit worth keeping
State your accuracy and your thresholds next to every map you publish. It
costs a sentence and it is the difference between a figure and a finding.
:::
